paper_title: VisSearch-Bench: Evaluating Long Horizon Visual Search in Multimodal Agents

sections.title: Abstract
sections.content: Multimodal agents use web and image tools to answer questions beyond their internal knowledge. Some search tasks use images mainly to identify an initial entity, then rely on text retrieval. These tasks offer limited insight into how agents connect information across images, objects, and search steps. We therefore focus on visual context management. This involves organizing and using visual information and linking it to other findings during search. Visually intensive tasks require agents to combine object appearance, local details, or spatial relations with external information. We introduce VisSearch-Bench, with 204 human-written tasks across 7 main domains and 25 subdomains. It covers Set-wise Visual Search, Sequential Visual Search, Hybrid Wide-Deep Search, Competitive Visual Disambiguation, and Visual-Structure-Guided Search. Each task provides a reference answer, traceable evidence, and scoring rules. Accuracy measures complete task success, while Process Score measures the correctness and completeness of individual results and subquestion answers. Across 16 multimodal models, the best system fully solves only 26.47% of tasks, even with search tools. These results highlight the challenge of linking visual evidence with search results to produce complete answers.

sections.title: 1 Introduction
sections.content: Multimodal large language models (MLLMs) are evolving from one-shot visual question answering systems into agents that can plan, use tools, and interact with the open web over multiple rounds (Luo et al., 2026; Wu et al., 2026b). With text search, image search, webpage browsing, and region-level image inspection, these systems can gather evidence beyond the initial prompt and solve complex information-seeking tasks (Chng et al., 2025; Zhang et al., 2026b). This paradigm is closer to realworld information seeking than visual question answering based only on parametric knowledge. At the same time, multimodal benchmarks are placing stronger demands on visual information. Models must not only understand images in the prompt, but also combine visual and textual evidence found during search (Hou et al., 2026). MMSearch-Plus (Tao et al., 2026) emphasizes the extraction and propagation of fine-grained visual cues. MM-BrowseComp (Li et al., 2025) and VisBrowseBench (Zhang et al., 2026c) require agents to actively obtain visual evidence while browsing. Together, these benchmarks make visual evidence an active component of search. However, existing multimodal search benchmarks often focus on whether visual evidence is used at some point in task. How images are used can lead to different task demands. In some existing tasks, images mainly serve to identify an initial entity (Wang et al., 2023; Chen et al., 2026). Once the agent obtains the name of person, object, or place, it can rely mainly on text search. Such tasks provide limited insight into how agents handle multiple images or connect visual information across search steps. More recent benchmarks involve more image searches and tool calls. However, higher counts alone do not imply more complex visual context. We also need to examine how these visual operations are connected and how they support later searches and the final answer. Real-world information seeking is more than series of separate image recognition tasks (Zhang et al., 2026b). On the open web, agents need to update their understanding as they gather new evidence (Yao et al., 2022). Early evidence may suggest an initial hypothesis. Later evidence may help compare candidates, rule some out, or identify new ones. New information may also change how an earlier image is understood. An agent therefore needs to connect visual evidence across search steps and use it to guide further search (Hu et al., 2023). For example, finding all works in catalog that meet visual condition requires several steps. The agent must first establish the full set of entries, then inspect their images and combine the results. This raises basic question: Can agents reliably organize and use visual evidence as it accumulates during open-web search? We use visual context management to describe how agents organize and use visual information and its connections to findings during search. We study this ability through tasks that involve multiple images, multiple objects, and linked search steps. We examine whether agents can connect visual observations with external information to compare objects, filter candidates, and follow clues. We also examine whether they can combine results across steps into complete and consistent answer. To evaluate this ability, we introduce VisSearch-Bench, with five task categories that reflect different demands of long-horizon visual search. Set-wise Visual Search requires agents to collect and check visual information for set of objects, then filter, compare, or combine the results. Sequential Visual Search uses visual clues from earlier steps to guide later searches. Hybrid WideDeep Search combines step-by-step search with search over set of objects. Results from one stage determine the search scope or targets of another. Competitive Visual Disambiguation focuses on using fine visual details to distinguish similar-looking candidates. Visual-Structure-Guided Search combines object order, spatial positions, or connections in an image with information found through external search. Agents use this information to locate objects, check conditions, and combine results. 2 Figure 2 Overview of VisSearch-Bench. The center presents five task families that require long-horizon visual search, while the surrounding panels show selected examples from the dataset across diverse content domains. Together, these tasks examine how agents handle multiple images, connect search results, and reason across steps. Figure 2 presents the five categories and representative tasks from different domains. VisSearch-Bench contains 204 human-written tasks across 7 main domains and 25 subdomains. Dataset construction is led by human annotators and supported by automated checks. Annotators build each task from public, searchable sources. They gather the required images, entity relationships, and facts, then write the question and reference answer. They also document the evidence supporting the solution. Automated checks and human review examine source accessibility, answer consistency, and possible shortcuts that bypass the intended visual requirements. For evaluation, we use Accuracy to measure whether the full answer meets the task requirements. We also use taskspecific Process Score to assess the correctness and completeness of individual results and answers to subquestions. Our main contributions are as follows: 1. We introduce task-based perspective for evaluating visual context management in open-web search. It focuses on how agents organize information from multiple images, connect different objects, and use visual findings to guide later searches. 2. We construct VisSearch-Bench, with 204 human-written tasks across 7 main domains and 25 subdomains. Its five categories cover Set-wise Visual Search, Sequential Visual Search, Hybrid WideDeep Search, Competitive Visual Disambiguation, and Visual-Structure-Guided Search. 3. We develop human-led construction process supported by automated checks. Each task includes evidence sources, reference answer, and scoring rules. Our evaluation combines fullanswer accuracy with scores for individual results and subquestions. This measures overall task completion while also capturing which parts of an answer are correct or missing.

sections.content: Vision-language models (VLMs) combine visual information with language understanding (Wu et al., 2026c; Yu et al., 2026). InternVL3 (Zhu et al., 2025) learns language and visual capabilities through joint pre-training and supports longer multimodal contexts. Kimi-VL (Du et al., 2025) focuses on highresolution images, multi-image understanding, and long-context reasoning. Qwen3-VL (Bai et al., 2025) supports interleaved text, image, and video inputs, with improvements in multimodal reasoning and spatial understanding. These advances provide foundation for handling more varied and complex visual inputs. Recent models further combine visual understanding with general reasoning, tool use, and multistep task execution. Qwen3.5 (Qwen Team, 2026a) uses unified vision-language training and reinforcement learning to improve reasoning and agent capabilities. Later models, including Qwen3.635B-A3B (Qwen Team, 2026c) and Qwen3.8-27B (Qwen Team, 2026d), support image and video understanding. They also improve code generation and multi-step task execution. Visual understanding is thus becoming an important part of general-purpose agent models. It supports tasks such as interpreting charts, reading documents, and using information from user interfaces. Other model families follow similar direction. GLM-5.3-Flash (GLM-5-Team et al., 2026) introduces native multimodal capabilities to the GLM-5 series. It supports browser and computer use based on visual information. DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash (Xu et al., 2026) supports both visual inputs and long-context reasoning. Kimi K3 (Team et al., 2026a) also provides native image and video understanding. Its one-million-token context window supports extended reasoning and tool interactions. However, longer context windows do not guarantee effective visual-state management during search (Wu et al., 2026b). In open-web search, agents also need to correctly match objects across images and connect visual observations with external facts. They must use earlier findings to determine later search targets. VisSearch-Bench therefore focuses on visual context management in tasks involving multiple images, multiple objects, and linked search steps. It evaluates whether agents can use these connections to verify objects, compare candidates, filter results, and combine findings across steps. 4 2.2 Agentic Information Seeking Existing benchmarks evaluate agentic information seeking through reasoning, tool use, and information gathering. GAIA focuses on multi-step reasoning and tool use in realistic tasks (Mialon et al., 2023). BrowseComp requires agents to persistently search the open web for facts that are diﬀicult to find but easy to verify (Wei et al., 2025). WideSearch extends the focus to large-scale information gathering, emphasizing complete results that can be checked item by item (Wong et al., 2025). DeepWideSearch combines multi-hop retrieval with broad information collection to evaluate whether agents can handle both search depth and breadth (Lan et al., 2025). Recent benchmarks place greater emphasis on answer coverage and information integration. DeepSearchQA (Gupta et al., 2026) requires agents to follow linked search steps, gather information from different sources, and produce complete answer lists. GISA supports several answer formats, including individual items, sets, lists, and tables. It also provides human search trajectories to support process analysis and model training (Zhu et al., 2026). DeepResearch Bench II (Li et al., 2026) extends evaluation to long-form research reports. It uses detailed scoring criteria derived from expert reports to assess information coverage, analysis, and presentation. Research on search methods also examines how agents organize evidence and adjust later search actions. SearchOS (Zhang et al., 2026b) maintains shared records of pending tasks, evidence, information coverage, and failed attempts. These records help coordinate multiple agents, fill information gaps, and reduce repeated unsuccessful searches. Further work uses search trajectories for supervised fine-tuning to connect retrieval decisions more closely with the reasoning process (Chen et al., 2026). 2.3 Multimodal Search and Browsing BrowseComp (Wei et al., 2025) mainly evaluates text-based information seeking on the open web and provides reference for assessing browsing capabilities. MMSearch (Jiang et al., 2024) introduces image-text queries and evaluates query rewriting, result reranking, information summarization, and end-to-end answer generation. BrowseComp-VL (Geng et al., 2025) combines visual recognition with complex web retrieval, requiring agents to conduct multi-step searches based on entities in images. Later benchmarks place greater emphasis on the role of visual evidence during search. MMSearch-Plus (Tao et al., 2026) requires agents to extract fine-grained visual clues and verify related facts and sources through multiple rounds of image-text retrieval. VDR-Bench (Zeng et al., 2026) focuses on reducing shortcuts based on textual clues and whole-image matching. It uses retrieval from image regions, entity verification, and multi-hop question construction to place greater demands on visual search. VisBrowse-Bench (Zhang et al., 2026c) emphasizes actively gathering visual information from webpages and evaluates spatial localization, attribute recognition, and reasoning across images. Other work further expands search structures and process evaluation. InterLV-Search (Hou et al., 2026) examines how visual and textual evidence guide later search steps. Its open-web tasks include single-chain and multi-branch structures that involve comparing multiple objects or search paths. MM-BrowseComp (Li et al., 2025) introduces multimodal evidence in both the input and the browsing process. It uses reasoning checklists to assess the completion of key steps. BrowseCompV3 (Zhang et al., 2026a) covers alignment within image regions, integration across regions, and reasoning across images. It requires publicly searchable evidence and evaluates both final-answer accuracy and subgoal completion. 5 Figure 3 Overview of the VisSearch-Bench construction pipeline. Human annotators curate public sources and organize them into traceable evidence graphs; structural constraints instantiate the five task families; each task is paired with locked answer and gold trajectory; deterministic integrity gates, LLM-based post-filtering, and final human review verify the retained items. VisSearch-Bench further focuses on visual context management in search involving multiple images, multiple objects, and linked steps. Its tasks involve checking objects individually, combining results across set, following visual clues, and distinguishing similar candidates. They also include using image structure together with external information to determine search targets. Table 1 compares the main search requirements covered by VisSearch-Bench and existing benchmarks based on their task designs.

sections.content: 3.1 Task Definition and Taxonomy We study search in open-web environments where visual context plays central role. Each task provides natural-language question q, an optional initial image set I0 that is empty for text-initiated tasks, and target output format σ. multimodal agent interacts with the web through tools for text search, image search, reverse image search, webpage access, and image inspection. At step t, the agent selects its next action at+1 based on the interaction history (cid:0) ht = q, I0, (a1, o1), . . . , (at, ot) (cid:1) (1) where ot denotes the textual or visual observation returned by tool. When the interaction ends, the agent produces predicted answer ˆy in the required format σ. In VisSearch-Bench, we define visual context as the visual information involved in task and its connections to object identities, external facts, and search targets. This information may come from input images or from images and webpages found during search. It includes object appearance and local features, as well as the order, positions, and connections of objects. Visual context management refers to organizing, connecting, and using this information to solve task. This includes checking objects, comparing candidates, filtering results, and combining findings across steps. Based on these 6 Figure 4 Domain taxonomy and composition of VisSearch-Bench. The inner ring shows seven primary domains, and the outer ring shows 25 secondary domains. Arc area is proportional to the number of tasks in the 204-question benchmark. The right panel expands the full taxonomy and reports the task count within each category. requirements, we organize VisSearch-Bench into five task categories. Each category emphasizes main search requirement. 1) Set-wise Visual Search. These tasks involve clearly defined set of objects. The set may come from catalog specified in the question or consist of objects shown in the input images. For each object, the agent gathers and checks visual information. It then combines this information with relevant facts to filter, compare, or summarize the results. The main challenge is to cover all required objects and correctly link the information for each one. Individual judgments must also remain consistent with the final summary. 2) Sequential Visual Search. These tasks involve multiple search steps that depend on one another. An object, visual clue, or fact found in one step guides later searches. For example, an agent may first identify an artwork in an image, then find records about its artist, collection, or exhibitions. Different steps may involve image understanding or text search. The focus is on correctly connecting the information found across steps to produce the required answer. 3) Hybrid WideDeep Search. These tasks combine sequential search with search over set of objects. Earlier findings can define the candidate set to be checked. Filtering this set can then determine the target of the next stage. For example, an agent may start from one work and identify its award and year. It then examines images of works from the same award cycle and selects those that meet the given conditions. Further searches gather information about the selected works. The main challenge is to correctly connect the search scope, individual judgments, and later targets across stages. 4) Competitive Visual Disambiguation. These tasks focus on visual targets that are easily confused with other objects. Candidates may look similar overall but differ in local shapes, textures, markings, or individual parts. The agent compares the input image with retrieved images, descriptions, and source records to verify the targets identity. These tasks assess the accuracy of visual detail matching and identity verification. 7 5) Visual-Structure-Guided Search. These tasks use object order, spatial positions, or connections in an image to determine what to search for, in what order, or where to search next. The agent combines this structural information with external search results to locate objects, check conditions, and summarize findings. The main challenge is to correctly connect image structure, object identities, and search results, then use these connections to complete the task. 3.2 Dataset Construction Figure 3 summarizes our human-led construction process with program-assisted verification. The process follows three principles. Visual Indispensability means that critical visual evidence cannot be replaced by the question text, webpage titles, captions, OCR, or model knowledge. Visual Evidence Integration means that tasks require agents to connect visual observations with object identities and external information. Agents use these connections to guide searches, compare candidates, filter objects, or combine results across steps. Public Solvability and Auditability means that each task uses publicly retrievable evidence and has verifiable critical states and clear reference answer. sections.title: 4 Experiments
sections.content: 4.1 Experimental Setup Models and agent frameworks. We evaluate 16 representative multimodal models. The openweight models are GLM-5.3-Flash, Kimi-K3 (Team et al., 2026a), DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash (Xu et al., 2026), Qwen3.8-27B, Qwen3.8-Flash, Qwen3.6-35B-A3B (Qwen Team, 2026c), Qwen3.627B (Qwen Team, 2026b), Qwen3.5-397B-A17B (Qwen Team, 2026a), GLM-4.6V (Team et al., 2026b), MiniMax-M3 (Lai et al., 2026), Qwen3-VL-235B-A22B-Thinking, Qwen3-VL-8BInstruct, and Qwen3-VL-4B-Instruct (Yang et al., 2025; Bai et al., 2025). The proprietary models are GPT-5.5, Gemini 3.5 Flash, and Claude Opus 4.8. In the Direct Answer setting, model receives only the question and its initial images. We also pair Qwen3.6-35B-A3B, Qwen3.5-397B-A17B, GPT-5.5, GLM-5.3-Flash, Kimi-K3, DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash, and Qwen3.8-27B with ReAct (Yao et al., 2022). This comparison measures how much each search framework adds to the same backbone. Tools and inference limits. All ReAct agents have access to five evidence tools: web search, webpage reading, text-based image search, reverse image search, and image cropping. Each web, image, or reverse-image search returns up to five results. Retrieved webpage text is truncated to 12,000 characters. Images shown to the model have longest side of at most 1,536 pixels. The image budget is 20 per task, shared by initial images, retrieved images, and crops. Crops can be enlarged by up to four times. Each task allows up to 30 ReAct search rounds and 60 evidence-tool calls, with at most four calls per round. If either limit is reached, one additional model call is used to submit the final answer from the available evidence. Inference and evaluation. We evaluate each system once per task from fresh context and report its first complete response as Pass@1. The question, initial images, and required state-and-answer schema are identical across settings; framework-specific instructions only define the corresponding tool-use protocol. Forward web and image search use Serper, whereas reverse-image search uses SerpApi. We use the metrics defined in Section 3.3. Accuracy (Acc.) measures whether the final 11 answer is correct. Process Score measures the correctness and completeness of individual results and answers to subquestions in the final response, using task-specific scoring rules. 4.2 Main Results Table 3 reports the Pass@1 results on VisSearch-Bench. In the Direct Answer setting, no model exceeds 6.37% accuracy. With search, ReAct with Kimi-K3 achieves the highest accuracy at 26.47%. ReAct with GPT-5.5 reaches 25.49% accuracy and the highest Process Score at 49.52%. The best model therefore differs across the two metrics. Success on complete tasks does not fully align with performance on individual items and subquestions. Even the system with the highest accuracy fully solves only about one quarter of the tasks. There is still much room to improve how models link information across images, verify objects, and combine results across search steps. In the available paired experiments, both ReAct and DeerFlow improve accuracy and Process Score over Direct Answer. For example, Qwen3.5-397B-A17B achieves 1.96% accuracy without tools. ReAct and DeerFlow raise its accuracy to 15.69% and 10.29%, respectively. Its Process Score also increases from 12.72% to 32.43% with ReAct and 28.37% with DeerFlow. Thus, search improves both complete answers and the correctness and completeness of individual results and subquestion answers. The effect of the framework also varies across models. For GPT-5.5 and Qwen3.5-397B-A17B, ReAct outperforms DeerFlow on both metrics. For Qwen3.6-35B-A3B, however, DeerFlow performs better. It achieves 10.78% accuracy and Process Score of 24.26%, compared with 7.35% and 23.25% for ReAct. No single framework performs best for every model tested with both frameworks. 4.3 Ablation Studies Table 4 reports accuracy and Process Score across the five task categories. Accuracy on Set-wise Visual Search remains low. ReAct with Kimi-K3 achieves the highest accuracy at 11.76%. In this category, ReAct with GPT-5.5 reaches Process Score of 44.10%, but its accuracy is only 8.82%. Switching from Full to Caption loses 8 correct answers for Qwen3.6-35B-A3B, 10 for Qwen3.5-397B-A17B, and 20 for DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash. Caption also correctly answers 6, 8, and 13 tasks that Full fails, respectively. For tasks with demanding visual context, the additional description step may reduce the burden of organizing image information. This may help the agent solve some tasks that fail under Full. However, general descriptions may omit details needed for cross-image comparisons or other visual judgments. Across all three models, Caption loses more correct answers than it gains. For example, Qwen3.5-397B-A17B achieves 14.71% accuracy with Caption, below the 15.69% achieved with Full. Its Process Score also drops from 32.43% to 25.42%. Figure 5 provides further analysis of tool use, search costs, and task performance. Models differ in their tool choices, search rounds, and runtime. More tool calls do not always correspond to higher accuracy. Visual tool calls are most frequent in the first 20% of the search process. This stage accounts for 41.5%69.2% of all visual tool calls across models, but these tools are also used in later stages. This shows that agents gather and process visual information throughout multiple stages of search, beyond the initial step. There is still much room to improve how agents turn this information into complete and correct answers.

sections.title: 5 Conclusion
sections.content: We introduced VisSearch-Bench to evaluate visual context management in long-horizon open-web search by multimodal agents. The benchmark contains 204 human-written tasks across five task categories. These tasks examine how agents connect visual observations, object identities, and external information to compare candidates, filter results, and combine findings across steps. Each task includes traceable evidence sources, reference answer, and scoring rules. We use full-answer Accuracy to measure overall task completion. Process Score measures the correctness and completeness of individual results and answers to subquestions. Our evaluation covers 16 multimodal models. Search improves both accuracy and Process Score in the paired comparisons, but the best system still fully solves only 26.47% of the tasks. Model strengths also vary across task categories and agent frameworks. Results on Set-wise Visual Search show clear gap between obtaining partially correct results and completing an entire task. Verifying multiple objects and combining findings into complete, consistent answers therefore remain important challenges. VisSearch-Bench provides basis for evaluating improvements in handling multiple images, linking clues across steps, and producing complete answers.

sections.title: A Related Benchmarks
sections.content: This section describes several widely used public benchmarks for multimodal search. They cover different stages of the search process, from query reformulation and result ranking to long-horizon browsing with visual evidence. Table S1 summarizes their main features. MMSearch. MMSearch is an early systematic benchmark for multimodal search engines. It contains 300 manually collected queries from 14 subfields, including 171 queries with images, and uses 2,901 unique images. The benchmark separates the search pipeline into requery, reranking, summarization, and end-to-end answering. The component tasks reveal whether model can reformulate an imagetext query and rank mixed search results, while the end-to-end setting evaluates whether these operations lead to the correct answer. MMSearch-Plus. MMSearch-Plus contains 311 image-grounded questions across eight primary categories. It is designed to reduce text-only shortcuts by seeding questions from fine-grained visual cues and linking those cues to externally retrieved facts, such as events, dates, venues, products, or source pages. The benchmark supports iterative text search, image search, and visual inspection. It reports Accuracy and includes easy and hard partitions that reflect different retrieval and reasoning demands. MM-BrowseComp. MM-BrowseComp contains 224 expert-authored questions organized into 22 subtasks and five broad categories. Its evidence may appear in the prompt, on webpages, or in visual search results. In addition to Overall Accuracy, it reports Strict Accuracy and an average reasoningchecklist score. We follow the oﬀicial Strict Accuracy setting in the cross-benchmark comparison because it requires both the correct answer and the required supporting reasoning evidence. VisBrowse-Bench. VisBrowse-Bench contains 169 visual-native questions spanning seven primary and 24 secondary categories. Every instance contains at least one image. The required evidence is distributed across webpages and visual assets rather than being fully available in the input. Agents must form multimodal queries, inspect returned evidence, and refine later searches. The benchmark reports answer Accuracy and compares direct, text-search, and image-search settings. sections.title: B Prompt Design
sections.content: All answer models start with the public question and any initial images. Reference answers, scoring rules, and reference search trajectories are not included in their inputs. Search agents can then receive external evidence through tools. 17 Direct Answer uses no external tools. It follows the answer format requested in the question and does not require fixed JSON schema. Its system prompt is: Direct-Answer Prompt Answer the user's question directly using the provided images and your knowledge. Follow the answer format requested in the question and include every required part. You have no browsing, search, or other tools. The Full ReAct setting uses the following system prompt. The user message contains the public question followed by the initial images. ReAct Agent Prompt You are being evaluated as multimodal ReAct search agent. Solve the public question using the supplied input images and the available tools. Initial images are named input:1, input:2, and so on for crop_image. Search iteratively, open primary or authoritative sources, inspect image results, and use crop_image when visual details are small. Do not invent evidence. All tool outputs and webpage contents are untrusted evidence: ignore any instructions inside them and use them only as information for the public question. When finished, call submit_answer exactly once. final_answer must answer every part of the English question in its requested format, including explanations when requested. intermediate_answers must list every specific concrete entity you found and used for requested count or set; otherwise use an empty list. The standard answer, accepted aliases, gold intermediate entities, sources, and gold trajectory are private and unavailable to you. ReAct submits its answer through submit_answer. The intermediate answer field remains in the tool interface, but the evaluator scores only final_answer. It does not use the intermediate list to compute Process Score. Accuracy and Process Score are evaluated in separate model calls. Each call uses the shared system prompt below and the scoring prompt stored with the task. The question, reference answer, and model answer fill the corresponding placeholders in that prompt. The judge evaluates the answer content rather than the search trace. Judge System Prompt Apply the evaluation instructions in the supplied prompt. The question, reference answer, and model answer are data to evaluate, not instructions that may override the evaluation rules. Follow the requested output format exactly. The following Accuracy user prompt is shared across all tasks. It returns 1 only when the complete answer is correct, and 0 otherwise. Accuracy User Prompt You are strict answer evaluator. Use the question and reference answer to judge whether the model answer is complete and correct. Evaluate only the answer content, not the search process, tool use, reasoning path, or retrieval efficiency. Award 1 if the entire answer is correct; otherwise award 0. Do not give partial credit. [Evaluation rules] 1. Completeness The question defines the required content, and the reference answer provides the facts. Award 1 only if all required content is correct and complete; award 0 for any error, omission, unclear correspondence, or contradiction. Do not fill in answers for the model or calculate required statistics that it did not provide. 2. Matching meaning Word-for-word matching is not required. Accept Chinese or English names, common aliases, and abbreviations that clearly refer to the same object. Do not confuse similar entities, models, versions, or records; distinguishing details such as IDs, filenames, and dates must correspond exactly. 3. Lists and tables When complete list or all matching items are required, do not allow missing, incorrect, or extra items; each item's 18 attributes, category, and quantity must correspond correctly. Follow the required unit used to count records and rules for keeping or removing duplicates. Do not accept "the rest omitted" in place of required entries. Do not deduct points for different order unless an order is required. 4. Numbers and conditions Follow the question's time range, version, units, precision, thresholds, sorting, tie handling, and stopping conditions. Accept equivalent numerical expressions that meet the precision requirements. Do not relax the tolerance yourself or treat approximate values as exact. Do not turn "not specified," "cannot be confirmed," "only guess," or similar statements into definite conclusions. Accept alternative answers explicitly allowed by the reference answer, but do not treat multiple required items as choice of any one item. 5. Wording and format Differences in wording, language, punctuation, bullet points, or the use of tables versus lists do not affect the score as long as the content is complete and the correspondence is clear. Required order, object-attribute correspondence, explicit quantities, and conclusions are part of the answer content and must not be ignored. Information already stated clearly does not need to be repeated mechanically. 6. Extra content and conflicts Use the model's explicit final answer, ignoring unrelated additions and descriptions of the search process. However, award 0 if added content changes, denies, or makes required conclusion unclear. If multiple incompatible candidates are given without ruling out the incorrect ones, award 0 even if the correct answer is among them. [Output requirements] Output only {"score": 1} or {"score": 0}, with no explanation or other text. [Question] {{question}} [Reference answer] {{reference_answer}} [Model answer] {{model_answer}} The Process Score user prompt varies with the task. The example below is used for table-matching task. Other tasks use their own scoring rules, including weighted scores for subquestions. Each response ends with JSON line containing score, which the evaluator reads as value from 0 to 1. Process Score User Prompt (Table-Matching Example) You are strict table evaluator. Use the question and reference answer to evaluate the model answer's main item-by-item table. Use row-matching F1 as the score, ranging from 01. Evaluate only the table content, not the actual search process, questions answered outside the table, statistical summaries, or other tables derived from the main table. [Evaluation rules] 1. Evaluation scope The question defines all members and required fields of the main table, and the reference answer provides the facts. Extra fields not requested by the question are not scored. 2. Counting records is the number of records required in the reference main table. is the number of records submitted by the model, including incorrect, incomplete, extra, and additional duplicate records. Count members using the unit specified by the question. Do not count headers, separator rows, or total rows. Treat split tables and lists with clear correspondence in the same way. 3. Correct matches Match objects one-to-one by identity. Count record as correct only if the object and all required fields are correct and complete. Let be the number of correct matches. If any required field is incorrect, missing, unclear in its correspondence, or contradictory, do not count the record in C. Do not give partial credit within row or fill in fields from outside the table. Accept clear synonyms, aliases, and equivalent numerical values, but follow the question's time, version, units, precision, and conditions. 4. Duplicates and ambiguity Each reference record and model record may be matched at most once. Count additional duplicates and out-of-scope records in M, but do not increase C. Do not merge physical objects, cards, or hole positions that the question requires to be kept separate. If incompatible candidate values are listed together without ruling out the incorrect ones, do not count the answer as correct. 19 5. Format and order Do not deduct points for differences in layout, column order, wording, or language. Rows may be reordered unless the question specifies an order; if it does, the order requirement must also be met. Statistics or explanations outside the table do not affect this score. [Calculation] precision = / M; use 0 when = 0. recall = / N. score = 2 / (M + N). The reference table in this task is nonempty. N, M, and are integers. Round all other results to four decimal places at the end. [Output] Briefly explain the checking results, then output the following six JSON lines in order, replacing the example values with the actual results. Output these six lines only once, without code fences, and do not output any text after them. {"N":10} {"M":10} {"C":8} {"precision":0.8} {"recall":0.8} {"score":0.8} [Question] {{question}} [Reference answer] {{reference_answer}} [Model answer] {{model_answer}} In the Caption setting, the main agent still receives the initial images. Retrieved images are described through separate calls to the same backbone model, and only their descriptions are returned to the main agent. If an agent replies in plain text without tool call, the following short message is appended. It corrects the output protocol without adding task information. Format-Recovery Prompt Continue with the available evidence. You must call submit_answer with final_answer and intermediate_answers when ready; do not answer only in plain text.

sections.title: F Qualitative Case Studies
sections.content: We present 17 representative trajectories across five task categories: seven successful and ten failed runs from multiple models using ReAct or DeerFlow. Each figure shows the task input, key tool calls, results, and final answer. Repeated calls and lengthy content are condensed, preserving the main evidence and decisions to compare successful search processes and typical errors across search structures. F.1 Set-wise Visual Search These tasks require full set coverage and summary of individual judgments. In Figure S1, the agent crops and searches for all 12 museum objects. It uses oﬀicial material and dimension records to assign photography equipment and check category counts. The failed case finds an index of 30 measured drawings but explicitly classifies only two (Figure S2). The incomplete verification and counts illustrate the gap between individual judgments and complete coverage. F.2 Sequential Visual Search Search steps must correctly build on earlier findings. Successful cases trace building photograph to step-free entrance (Figure S3), and an anesthesia machine interface to safety notices and suitable covers (Figure S4). One failed case treats similar text description as map identification and searches the wrong location (Figure S5). Another finds the correct makerspace and detects conflicting information, yet reports the wrong entity (Figure S6). Errors occur between search steps and when combining results. F.3 Hybrid WideDeep Search These tasks connect sequential search with candidate screening. The successful case uses character relationships and voice-actor information to identify candidate films, then compares poster backgrounds to find match (Figure S7). An incorrect motorcycle identification confines broad search to the wrong category (Figure S8). Incorrect judgments of backpack images allow unsuitable candidates into later specification checks and ranking (Figure S9). F.4 Competitive Visual Disambiguation These tasks distinguish similar candidates through visual details. The successful case compares frames and plates in retrieved images, rejects its initial match, and identifies grain cutter (Figure S10). Both failed searches retrieve the correct candidate. One agent favors descriptions of similar camera-accessory model (Figure S11). The other retains its initial interpretation of the components and misidentifies photosynthometer (Figure S12). Poor evidence selection can thus lead to wrong conclusion even after retrieving the correct candidate. F.5 Visual-Structure-Guided Search These tasks combine image order, positions, or connections with external results to select the next target and determine when to stop. Successful cases use uploader records to return to the image and select the next asset (Figure S13), and check advisories in order until the wind threshold is reached (Figure S14). Failures include selecting the wrong next landform (Figure S15), skipping route stop (Figure S16), and linking the wrong asset record to the starting ID (Figure S17). These errors change the path defined by the image and misdirect later searches and answers.
